title: VIII. The Evidence Of The Witnesses. The Babe
paragraphs: Now the questioning of the witnesses began. But we will not tell it in as much detail as we did before. We will skip how Nikolay Parfenovitch urged each witness to speak truthfully and according to his conscience, and told him he would later have to repeat his statement under oath. We will skip how each witness had to sign the protocol of what he had said, and the rest of the formalities. We will only say that the questioning kept returning to one point above all: the three thousand roubles. Had Mitya spent three thousand here at Mokroe the first time, a month earlier, or only fifteen hundred? And had he spent three thousand yesterday, or fifteen hundred? Alas, every witness’s testimony went against Mitya. Not one spoke for him, and some even offered new facts, almost crushing ones, that flatly contradicted Mitya’s own account.

Trifon Borissovitch was the first witness. He was not the least bit abashed in front of the lawyers. If anything, he looked sternly and severely indignant at the accused, and this made him seem honest and dignified. He said little and kept himself in reserve. He waited to be asked, and then answered precisely and without hurrying. He stated firmly and without any hesitation that the sum spent a month ago could not have been less than three thousand. All the peasants round here, he said, would swear they had heard Dmitri Fyodorovitch himself speak of three thousand. “And what a lot of money he threw away on the gypsy girls alone! A thousand went on them alone, I’d say.”
“I don’t think I gave them even five hundred,” Mitya muttered gloomily. “Pity I didn’t count the money at the time, but I was drunk....”
Mitya sat sideways, with his back to the curtains. He listened with a dark, tired, wretched look, as if to say:
“Oh, say whatever you like. It doesn’t matter now.”

“More than a thousand went on them, Dmitri Fyodorovitch,” said Trifon Borissovitch firmly. “You scattered it around any old how, and they scooped it up. A thieving, rascally bunch they were, horse-stealers. They’ve been chased out of here, or maybe they’d tell you themselves how much they got from you. I saw that money in your hands with my own eyes—count it I didn’t, you wouldn’t let me, that’s true—but going by the look of it, I’d say it was far more than fifteen hundred ... fifteen hundred, ha! We’ve seen money too. We know how to judge a sum....”
About the money spent yesterday, he said that Dmitri Fyodorovitch had told him the moment he arrived that he had brought three thousand with him.
“Come now, Trifon Borissovitch, is that really so?” Mitya answered. “I can’t have said so definitely that I’d brought three thousand?”

“You said it, Dmitri Fyodorovitch. You said it with Andrey there. Andrey’s still here himself. Send for him. And out in the hall, when you were treating the chorus, you shouted for everyone to hear that you’d leave your sixth thousand here—meaning, we have to understand, together with what you spent before. Stepan and Semyon heard it, and Pyotr Fomitch Kalganov was standing next to you then, too. Maybe he’ll remember it....”

This evidence about the “sixth” thousand made an extraordinary impression on both lawyers. They were delighted with the new way of counting. Three thousand and three thousand made six. Three then and three now, six in all. It was plain.

They questioned all the peasants Trifon Borissovitch had named: Stepan and Semyon, the driver Andrey, and Kalganov. The peasants and the driver backed up Trifon Borissovitch’s story without a moment’s doubt. They wrote down with special care Andrey’s report of what Mitya had said to him on the road: “‘Where am I going,’ he says, ‘Dmitri Fyodorovitch, to heaven or to hell? And shall I be forgiven in the next world or not?’”
Ippolit Kirillovitch, the psychologist, listened with a subtle smile. He finished by recommending that these remarks about where Dmitri Fyodorovitch was going be “included in the case.”

When Kalganov was called, he came in unwillingly, scowling and in a foul mood. He talked to the lawyers as if he had never set eyes on them, though they were acquaintances he had met every day for a long time. He began by saying that “he knew nothing about it and didn’t want to.” But it turned out he had heard of the “sixth” thousand, and he admitted he had been standing close by when it was said. As far as he could tell, he “didn’t know” how much money Mitya had in his hands. He stated that the Poles had cheated at cards. Pressed again and again, he said that once the Poles had been thrown out, Mitya’s standing with Agrafena Alexandrovna had certainly got better, and that she had said she loved him. He spoke of Agrafena Alexandrovna with reserve and respect, as if she were a lady of the best society, and not once did he let himself call her Grushenka. The young man plainly loathed giving evidence, yet Ippolit Kirillovitch questioned him at great length, and it was from him alone that he learned every detail of Mitya’s “romance,” so to speak, that night. Mitya never once interrupted Kalganov. At last they let the young man go, and he walked out of the room in undisguised indignation.

The Poles were questioned as well. They had gone to bed in their room, but they had lain awake all night. When the police officers arrived, they dressed hurriedly and were ready, knowing they would surely be sent for. They gave their testimony with dignity, though not without some nervousness. The little Pole turned out to be a retired official of the twelfth class who had served in Siberia as a veterinary surgeon. His name was Mussyalovitch. Pan Vrublevsky turned out to be a dentist without a certificate. Nikolay Parfenovitch put the questions to them as they came in, but both addressed their answers to Mihail Makarovitch, who stood off to one side. In their ignorance they took him for the most important man there, the one in command, and at every word they called him “Pan Colonel.” Only after Mihail Makarovitch himself corrected them several times did they understand that their answers were to go to Nikolay Parfenovitch alone. It turned out that they spoke perfectly correct Russian, except for an accent on certain words. When Pan Mussyalovitch spoke of his relations with Grushenka, past and present, he did it proudly and warmly. Mitya flared up on the spot and declared that he would not let that “scoundrel” talk like that in his presence! Pan Mussyalovitch at once pointed out the word “scoundrel” and asked that it be entered in the protocol. Mitya was boiling with rage.
“He’s a scoundrel! A scoundrel! Put that down. And put down, too, that whatever the protocol says, I still call him a scoundrel!” he shouted.

Nikolay Parfenovitch did enter this in the protocol, but he showed the most commendable tact and skill. He sternly reprimanded Mitya, then cut short every further question about the romantic side of the case and hurried on to what mattered. One part of the Poles’ evidence stirred the lawyers’ special interest. In that very room Mitya had tried to buy off Pan Mussyalovitch. He had offered him three thousand roubles to give up his claims: seven hundred roubles at once, and the other two thousand three hundred “to be paid next day in the town.” At the time he had sworn he did not have the whole sum with him at Mokroe, but that his money was in the town. Mitya said hotly that he had not said he would surely pay the rest next day in the town. But Pan Vrublevsky confirmed it. Mitya thought a moment, then admitted with a frown that it must have been as the Poles said, that he had been worked up at the time and might well have said it.

The prosecutor seized on this piece of evidence. It seemed to establish for the prosecution (and in fact they did draw this conclusion from it) that half of the three thousand that had come into Mitya’s hands, or at least part of it, might truly have been left hidden somewhere in the town, or even somewhere here in Mokroe. That would explain what had puzzled the prosecution so much: why only eight hundred roubles were found on Mitya. Small as it was, this fact had been the one piece of evidence that had so far counted somewhat in Mitya’s favor. Now it had fallen apart. The prosecutor asked where he would have found the remaining two thousand three hundred roubles, given that he himself denied having more than fifteen hundred. Mitya answered confidently that he had meant to offer the “little chap” no money at all, but a formal deed transferring his rights to the village of Tchermashnya, the same rights he had already offered to Samsonov and Madame Hohlakov. The prosecutor actually smiled at “the innocence of this dodge.”
“And you imagine he would have taken such a deed in place of two thousand three hundred roubles cash?”

“He would certainly have taken it,” Mitya said warmly. “Why, look, he could have grabbed not two thousand but four or six for it. He’d have set his lawyers on the job, Poles and Jews, and he might have got not three thousand but the whole estate out of the old man.”

Pan Mussyalovitch’s evidence was, of course, entered in the protocol in the fullest detail. Then the Poles were let go. The business of the cheating at cards was barely touched. Nikolay Parfenovitch was far too pleased with them already, and he did not want to trouble them over trifles. Besides, it was only a stupid, drunken quarrel over cards. There had been plenty of drinking and disorder that night.... So the two hundred roubles stayed in the Poles’ pockets.

Next old Maximov was called in. He came in timidly, with little steps, looking very rumpled and low in spirits. All this while he had been sheltering downstairs with Grushenka, sitting dumbly beside her. “Now and then he’d start blubbering over her and wiping his eyes with a blue check handkerchief,” as Mihail Makarovitch told it afterwards. So in the end she had been trying to soothe and comfort him herself. The old man admitted at once that he had done wrong. He had borrowed “ten roubles in my poverty” from Dmitri Fyodorovitch, he said, and he was ready to pay it back. Nikolay Parfenovitch asked him point-blank whether he had noticed how much money Dmitri Fyodorovitch had in his hand, since he must have seen the amount better than anyone when he took the note from him. Maximov declared in the most positive manner that there was twenty thousand.
“Have you ever seen as much as twenty thousand before, then?” Nikolay Parfenovitch asked with a smile.

“Of course I have. Not twenty, but seven, when my wife mortgaged my little property. She’d only let me look at it from a distance, and she boasted about it to me. It was a very thick bundle, all rainbow-colored notes. And Dmitri Fyodorovitch’s were all rainbow-colored....”

They did not keep him long. At last Grushenka’s turn came. Nikolay Parfenovitch was plainly nervous about what her appearance might do to Mitya, and he muttered a few words of caution to him. But Mitya only bowed his head in silence, letting him understand “that he would not make a scene.” Mihail Makarovitch himself brought Grushenka in. She came in with a stern, gloomy face that looked almost calm, and sat quietly in the chair Nikolay Parfenovitch offered her. She was very pale and seemed to be cold, and she drew her magnificent black shawl tightly around her. She had a slight feverish chill—the first sign of the long illness that followed that night. Her serious air, her direct, earnest look and her quiet manner made a very favorable impression on everyone. Nikolay Parfenovitch was even a little “fascinated.” Talking about it afterwards, he admitted that only then had he seen “how handsome the woman was.” He had seen her several times before, but he had always thought of her as something of a “provincial hetaira.” “She has the manners of the best society,” he said with enthusiasm, gossiping about her in a circle of ladies. But the ladies took this with real indignation and promptly called him a “naughty man,” to his great delight.

Coming into the room, Grushenka gave Mitya just one quick glance. He looked back at her anxiously, but her face calmed him at once. After the usual first questions and cautions, Nikolay Parfenovitch asked her, a little hesitantly but with perfect courtesy, how she stood with the retired lieutenant Dmitri Fyodorovitch Karamazov. Grushenka answered firmly and quietly:

“He was an acquaintance. He visited me as an acquaintance this past month.” To further prying questions she gave plain, completely frank answers. She said that “at times” she had found him attractive, but that she had never loved him. She had won his heart, and his old father’s as well, “out of my own nasty spite.” She had noticed that Mitya was terribly jealous of Fyodor Pavlovitch and of everyone else, but that had only amused her. She had never meant to go to Fyodor Pavlovitch; she had only been laughing at him. “I had no thoughts for either of them this whole month. I was waiting for another man, one who had wronged me. But I think,” she finished, “you needn’t ask about that, and I needn’t answer, because it’s my own business.”

Nikolay Parfenovitch took the hint immediately. Once more he put the “romantic” side of the case aside and turned to the serious matter, the one that counted most, the three thousand roubles. Grushenka agreed that three thousand roubles had certainly been spent at the first carousal at Mokroe. She had not counted the money herself, but she had heard it was three thousand from Dmitri Fyodorovitch’s own mouth.
“Did he tell you so only when you were alone, or in front of somebody else? Or did you merely hear him say it to other people while you were present?” the prosecutor put in at once.
Grushenka answered that she had heard him say it in front of other people, and had also heard him say it when they were alone.
“Did he tell you so just once when you were alone, or several times?” asked the prosecutor, and found out that he had told Grushenka so several times.
Ippolit Kirillovitch was very pleased with this evidence. More questions brought out that Grushenka also knew where the money had come from: Dmitri Fyodorovitch had got it from Katerina Ivanovna.
“And have you never once heard that the money spent a month ago was not three thousand but less, and that Dmitri Fyodorovitch had set half of that sum aside for himself?”
“No, I never heard that,” Grushenka replied.
It was made clear, further, that Mitya had often told her the opposite: that he hadn’t a penny.
“He was always hoping to get some from his father,” Grushenka added at the end.
“Did he ever say in your hearing ... in passing, or in a fit of temper,” Nikolay Parfenovitch broke in suddenly, “that he meant to make an attempt on his father’s life?”
“Ach, yes, he said that,” Grushenka sighed.
“Once, or more than once?”
“More than once. Always when he was angry.”
“And did you believe he would do it?”
“No, I never believed it,” she said firmly. “I trusted his noble heart.”
“Gentlemen, permit me,” Mitya cried suddenly, “permit me to say a single word to Agrafena Alexandrovna, with you here.”
“Go ahead and speak,” Nikolay Parfenovitch allowed.
“Agrafena Alexandrovna!” Mitya rose from his chair. “Believe in God and believe in me. I am not guilty of my father’s murder!”

After saying this, Mitya sat back down. Grushenka stood up and crossed herself devoutly before the icon. “Thank You, O Lord,” she said, her voice trembling with feeling. Still standing, she turned to Nikolay Parfenovitch and added:

“Believe him, now that he’s said it like that! I know him. He’ll say anything for a joke or out of stubbornness, but he’ll never lie to you against his conscience. He’s telling you the whole truth. You can believe it.”
“Thank you, Agrafena Alexandrovna. You’ve given me new courage,” Mitya answered in a shaking voice.

About the money spent the day before, she said she did not know how much it was, but she had heard him tell several people he had three thousand on him. Asked where he got the money, she said he had told her he “stole” it from Katerina Ivanovna. She had told him in reply that he hadn’t stolen it, and that he must pay it back the next day. The prosecutor pressed her hard: was the money he said he had stolen from Katerina Ivanovna what he spent yesterday, or what he squandered here a month ago? She declared that he meant the money spent a month ago, and that this was how she had understood him.

At last Grushenka was free to go. On a sudden impulse, Nikolay Parfenovitch told her she could go back to town at once, and that if he could help her in any way, with horses for instance, or if she wanted an escort, he ... would be—

“I thank you sincerely,” said Grushenka with a bow. “I’m going with this old gentleman. I’m taking him back to town with me. In the meantime, if you’ll let me, I’ll wait downstairs to hear what you decide about Dmitri Fyodorovitch.”

She left. Mitya was calm and even looked more cheerful, but only for a moment. A strange bodily weakness was weighing on him more and more. His eyes were closing from exhaustion. The questioning of the witnesses was at last over. They began the final review of the protocol. Mitya stood up, went from his chair to the corner by the curtain, lay down on a big chest covered with a rug, and fell fast asleep at once.
He had a strange dream, one that had nothing to do with the place or the hour.

He was riding somewhere in the steppes where he had once been stationed, and a peasant was driving him in a cart with a pair of horses, through snow and sleet. He was cold. It was early November, and the snow came down in big wet flakes that melted the moment they hit the ground. The peasant drove him at a smart pace. He had a long fair beard. He was not old, perhaps fifty, and wore a gray peasant smock. A village lay not far ahead. He could see the black huts, and half of them had burned down, with only charred beams left standing. As they drove in, peasant women were lined up along the road, a great many of them, a whole row, all thin and wan, their faces a kind of brownish color. The one at the end was the worst, a tall, bony woman who looked forty but could have been only twenty, with a long, thin face. In her arms a small baby was crying. Her breasts looked so dried up that there could not be a drop of milk in them. The child cried and cried and stretched out its little bare arms, with fists blue from the cold.
“Why are they crying? Why are they crying?” Mitya asked as they dashed cheerfully past.
“It’s the babe,” the driver answered. “The babe is weeping.”
Mitya was struck by the way he said “the babe,” in his peasant fashion, and he liked that the peasant called it a “babe.” It seemed to hold more pity.
“But why is it weeping?” Mitya kept asking stupidly. “Why are its little arms bare? Why don’t they wrap it up?”
“The babe is cold. Its little clothes are frozen through and give no warmth.”
“But why? Why is it so?” foolish Mitya went on.
“Well, they’re poor folk, burnt out. They’ve no bread. They’re begging because they were burnt out.”

“No, no,” said Mitya, still seeming not to understand. “Tell me why those poor mothers are standing there. Why are people poor? Why is the babe poor? Why is the steppe bare? Why don’t they hug and kiss each other? Why don’t they sing joyful songs? Why are they so dark from black misery? Why don’t they feed the babe?”

He knew that his questions made no sense and were foolish, and yet he wanted to ask exactly these, and he had to ask them exactly this way. He felt a passion of pity rising in his heart, such as he had never known. He wanted to weep. He wanted to do something for all of them, so that the babe would cry no more, so that the dark-faced, dried-up mother would cry no more, so that from that moment no one would shed another tear. And he wanted to do it at once, right now, whatever stood in his way, with all the recklessness of the Karamazovs.

“And I’ll go with you. I won’t leave you ever again, not for the rest of my life. I’m coming with you,” he heard Grushenka’s tender voice beside him, trembling with feeling. And his heart glowed, and he pushed forward toward the light, and he longed to live, to live, to go on and on toward the new, beckoning light, and to hurry, hurry, now, at once!

“What! Where?” he exclaimed, opening his eyes and sitting up on the chest, smiling brightly, as if he had come to after a faint. Nikolay Parfenovitch was standing over him, proposing that he hear the protocol read aloud and sign it. Mitya figured he had slept an hour or more, but he did not hear a word Nikolay Parfenovitch said. All at once he was struck by a pillow under his head. It had not been there when he lay back, worn out, on the chest.
“Who put that pillow under my head? Who was so kind?” he cried, in a kind of rapturous gratitude, with tears in his voice, as though someone had done him a great kindness.

He never learned who the kind person was. Maybe one of the peasant witnesses, or Nikolay Parfenovitch’s little secretary, had felt sorry for him and thought to slip a pillow under his head. But his whole soul trembled with tears. He walked to the table and said he would sign whatever they wanted.
“I’ve had a good dream, gentlemen,” he said in a strange voice, with a new light in his face, as of joy.
